web_title: 9. Bull vs. Bear, Portfolio Action & Redeployment Plan
book_title: Chapter 9: Bull vs. Bear, Likely Outcomes & Our Action Plan
title: Right Company, Priced for the Best Case
question: Given the business we found and the price we are asked to pay, what do we do with new capital today, what do we do with any holding, and what would change our mind?

epigraph.quote: “Price is what you pay; value is what you get.”
epigraph.author: Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letter for 2008, quoting Ben Graham

web_blocks.html: Our new-capital verdict on Xpro India is REJECTED. It is a verdict about price, not about the business. The 12 November 2026 close was ₹1,142.20. Pass 1 rated the business CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL with KPI health PASS_WITH_WATCH [2][30][8]. That means a survivor with clean accounts, an A-/A1 rating and a real specialty-film franchise. Its returns on capital stay below its cost of capital until two new film lines fill. The shares already pay for that outcome. Market capitalisation is ₹2,681 Cr. The stock trades at 76.0x trailing earnings and 3.46x book value on a 3.8% ROCE (Chapter 7). Our probability-weighted value is ₹865 a share, 24.3% below the close. Even a pullback into the technical support zone of ₹1,105.6 to ₹1,150.6 leaves the ₹811 base-case value below the entry price [4][10]. That fails the 1.5:1 reward-to-risk gate that separates a patient wait from a rejection. So we reject rather than hedge.

web_blocks.title: The bull case, in its strongest honest form

web_blocks.html: The bull case has four legs, and each is real. Scarcity and import substitution. India imports about 70% of its base capacitor film [42]. Xpro says it supplies about a third of domestic demand [3]. Its platform goes from 4,000 t to 13,000 t between 2025 and 2027 if the UAE line starts [2]. The customers are capacitor makers that cannot qualify a new film quickly. Chapter 4 showed real qualification friction at the thin-gauge end.

The numbers are turning. Q2 FY2027 revenue was ₹176.7 Cr, up 47.4%. Dielectric revenue rose 64%, and output on the new Barjora line rose 35% on the quarter. Management says the line turned EBITDA-positive in October. It expects 70-80% utilisation in the March 2027 quarter [3][6]. The balance sheet can carry the build. Cash and bank balances were ₹233.4 Cr against ₹273.7 Cr of borrowings at 30 September 2026 [14]. Net debt excluding leases is therefore ₹40.3 Cr. The debt is export-credit backed. Management does not anticipate raising equity for the current programme or the UAE unit [3]. Lines 4 and 5 are only on the roadmap [2]. Operating leverage is large. Each 1,000 t of dielectric film at ₹430/kg is ₹43.0 Cr of revenue (our calculation). At a 30% margin that is ₹12.9 Cr of EBITDA. The cost base is already in the P&L.

Put the pieces together. If management's own ranges hold, group PAT is about ₹106 Cr. Those ranges are a 35% dielectric margin on the new-line revenue and 6% on Coex. Today's market capitalisation is then 25.3x that profit (our calculation, Chapter 7). A bull would call that a fair-to-full price for a scarce asset in a growing niche. A bull would also buy a doubled platform before the proof arrives.

web_blocks.title: The bear case, in its strongest honest form

web_blocks.html: The price pays for the success case in full. The stock trades at 76.0x trailing earnings, 48.7x enterprise value to trailing operating profit and 3.46x book. That is above every profitable peer in the comparison (Chapter 7) [10]. Garware Hi-Tech Films trades at 41x with a 20.9% operating margin and an 18.1% ROCE. SRF trades at 32x with 18.8% and 14.6%. Since March 2023 the price is up 65% while earnings per share are down 67% [40][17]. The whole gain is multiple expansion on an unfinished project.

Returns are below the cost of capital, and the central case does not fix that. ROIC was 20.7% in FY2023 and 3.4% in FY2026, against our assumed 12% cost of capital. The central case earns ₹141 Cr of EBITDA and ₹68 Cr of PAT. That is about 8.8% on roughly ₹830 Cr of invested capital (Chapters 5 and 6). The implied dielectric EBITDA margin is 16-23% in FY2026 if the Coex range of 5-7% is right. Management quotes 35-55%. EBITDA per tonne is down 46% since FY2023 [2][36].

The supply side is filling. Indian capacitor-film nameplate that could serve the market is about 22,500 t. That is Xpro 8,000 t, JPFL Films 10,000 t and SRF 4,500 t. Demand is about 15,000 t [113][7]. Imports enter at zero duty. SRF went from trial runs to customer approvals in two to three quarters. Xpro itself cut dielectric prices 6-7% in FY2025 [41]. The failure case is not hypothetical. Chapter 4's Jindal and Treofan parallel built capacity into a market that did not need it. Its operating margin went from 24.2% to roughly zero.

Execution and concentration. Barjora Line 2 started about 15 months after the promised date. The UAE line is 18-21 months behind its first public schedule. Euro debt of about EUR 25 mn is largely unhedged. It produced a ₹15.8 Cr consolidated FX loss in FY2026 [2][8]. One unnamed customer is 29.6% of revenue. The Managing Director who built the programme retires on 31 December 2026 [88]. A stock that has fallen 50% twice in four years on slipped dates can do it a third time.

web_blocks.takeaway: The weighted value of ₹865 is 24.3% below the close, an annualised loss of about 18% over the 1.4 years to 31 March 2028. The 12% cost-of-capital hurdle over the same period would need ₹1,336 (Chapter 7 and 9 arithmetic) [4].

web_blocks.html: Convention and the bear case. Each value is a price at 31 March 2028 that capitalises FY2029E earnings, a one-year-forward multiple. Chapter 7's reverse DCF asks a different question, so it uses March 2029 and March 2030 by design. The bear case sits below the trailing profit of ₹34.9 Cr because the new lines add about ₹38 Cr of annual depreciation and interest. That is ₹42 Cr and ₹16 Cr against ₹12.0 Cr and ₹7.5 Cr in FY2026 (our calculation), while the margin stays near the 16-23% implied for FY2026.

The weights come from reference cases and the company's own record, not from hope. Those are small samples, so treat 30% / 50% / 20% as judgment and read the stress tests that follow. Management has missed every commissioning date it has set (Chapter 5). The Indian film cycle has twice built capacity into a soft market (Chapters 1 and 4). The Jindal and Treofan twin failed on exactly this pattern. That supports a 30% bear weight. The base case needs the new lines to ramp at roughly management's guided pace, at the Chapter 5 central margin. It receives half the weight. The bull case needs management's full range to be met early and thin-gauge pricing to arrive. It gets 20%.

Three cross-checks follow. First, hold the bear weight at 30%. The bull case would then need a 52.2% probability for the weighted value to equal today's close. We assign 20%. Second, assume management is right. Re-base the base case to the management-range PAT of ₹106 Cr, which is ₹1,265 at 28x. Re-weight to 20% / 55% / 25%. The value is ₹1,197, only 4.8% above the close. Earning 12% a year over 1.4 years (17.0% in total) on that value needs an entry near ₹1,023. Third, the result does not depend on the 28x multiple. At 22x on the base case the weighted value is ₹778, 31.9% below the close. At 32x it is ₹923, 19.2% below. If Xpro delivers its guidance, the stock is fairly valued, not cheap. In every other world it is not.

web_blocks.takeaway: Quality of business is not the objection on any horizon. The objection is paying a 76x multiple for a project whose proof arrives in 2027.

web_blocks.title: New-capital verdict and the levels that matter

web_blocks.html: The verdict is REJECTED. The anti-hedging rule asks a simple question. If we wait for the price to fall to technical support, is the expected return positive and asymmetric? The support zone is ₹1,105.6-1,150.6 [10]. Our base-case value of ₹811 is below the bottom of it. Waiting for support therefore does not fix the arithmetic. The business is not a fundamental failure (CYCLICAL_CONDITIONAL, not FUNDAMENTAL_FAIL). This is a valuation rejection, and it is reversible by price or by evidence.

Re-underwriting zone, not an order. At ₹660 the base-case reward is ₹151 against ₹100 of risk to a ₹560 stop. That is 1.51:1. At ₹620 it is 3.18:1. At ₹660 the weighted value is 31.0% above the entry. This is the zone where our own numbers would clear the gate. The ₹560 stop is a valuation stop. It is set 15% below the ₹660 top of the zone (₹561 before rounding; our calculation). The zone sits far below every technical support level, so no chart level can anchor a stop. The bear value of ₹414 is below the stop, so the stop limits the loss only if the price does not gap through it. The targets are ₹414 (bear), ₹811 (base) and ₹1,674 (bull). The zone is far below the 12 November close and below the March 2026 closing low of ₹813.0. That shows how much of the project the price has already discounted. We do not forecast that the price will go there.

The evidence route. A cheaper route back is evidence. Barjora Line 2 would need 70% or more utilisation in the March 2027 quarter. The UAE line would need to be capitalised on time. Dielectric margin would need to be disclosed above 30%, and the customer base should no longer be 29.6% one name. That evidence would lift our base case towards the management-range value. The weighted value would rise to about ₹1,197. That supports buying only near ₹1,023 for a 12% annual return.

The 13 November print. The TradingView snapshot pulled after the 13 November close shows ₹1,190.10 (+4.19%). Volume was 0.6x average. The close was 4.2% above the 12 November close and just under the ₹1,195.66 30-week average [10]. Against that print the weighted value is -27.4%. The verdict is unchanged.

The same-session positions ledger lists 18 Zerodha positions with a market value of ₹37.2 lakh. XPROINDIA is not among them [4]. The holding action is therefore NOT_HELD. Zero shares are to be sold, and there is no stop to ratchet. We do not infer holdings from any other source. If shares sit in an account outside this ledger, treat a daily close below ₹1,105 as the first review line. Treat the ₹960-940 zone as the second. The valuation arithmetic above still applies to any added capital. This is an advisory alert, not a broker order.

web_blocks.takeaway: No alert requires a sale because nothing is held. Each one is a reason to re-underwrite, not to buy.

web_blocks.title: Redeployment: the next marginal cash unit

web_blocks.html: There is no pool of money being freed, so the capital under review is the next marginal cash unit. We allocate 100% to cash, 0% to the active shortlist and 0% to outside candidates. This run did not underwrite any alternative to the same standard. An unfunded alternative with an unverified setup is worse than cash earning a deposit rate. Equity destinations are funded only when three things exist for that name. These are a current-session snapshot, a documented business verdict and a 1.5:1 asymmetry. The full destination table and the position-sizing rules follow this chapter.
There is also no options expression. XPROINDIA is not in the NSE F&O segment, so no listed call spread or LEAPS exists. Any view has to be expressed in cash equity, which the verdict above declines.

Re-underwrite Xpro India when any one of these occurs. The price enters ₹620-660. Or Barjora Line 2 reports 70%+ utilisation with a disclosed dielectric margin above 30% and the UAE line is capitalised, with the price near ₹1,020 or lower. Or a weekly close above ₹1,200 on weekly volume of at least 1.5x the average week pairs with a Q3 FY2027 result that lifts the central case.

book_paragraphs: Let me put two analysts at the table with you, one who loves this business and one who has been burned by businesses like it. The first says: look at the revenue, up 47% in the September quarter, look at the new line making money, look at a balance sheet that is nearly debt-free. The second says: look at the price. Both are right, and our job is to work out what each fact is worth in rupees per share. I would like you to follow that arithmetic with me, because the answer is not a matter of mood.

Start with what the bull gets right. India imports about 70% of its capacitor film, and Xpro is the one domestic maker with a real platform, 13,000 tonnes by 2027 if the UAE plant starts [42][2]. The Managing Director told the November call that “we expect during the fourth quarter this year to be operating the new line at between 70% to 80% of its rated capacity” [3]. If that happens, each extra thousand tonnes sold at ₹430 a kilo adds ₹43.0 Cr of revenue and about ₹12.9 Cr of EBITDA at a 30% margin, and most of the cost is already in the accounts. Run management's own ranges and you get a profit of about ₹106 Cr, and today's value of the whole company is 25 times that.

Now ask what the bear gets right, because it is more than people expect. The stock trades at 76 times last year's earnings and 3.5 times book value, on a business that earned 3.8% on its capital in the latest year. Garware, a specialty-film maker earning an 18% return on capital, trades at 41 times; SRF, with a 15% return, trades at 32 times [10]. Since March 2023 the shares have risen 65% while earnings per share fell 67%, which means every rupee of that gain is hope, not profit [40][17].

Return on capital is the heart of it. Chapter 6 showed that the company earned about 21% on its invested capital in FY2023 and only 3.4% in FY2026, because roughly ₹700 Cr was poured into two film lines that are not yet full [8]. Even in our central case, with Barjora's new line at 80% and the UAE line at 50%, the return reaches about 8.8%, still below the 12% a shareholder should demand. Charlie Munger's advice was “Invert, always invert.” So invert: how would an investor lose money here? By paying for the central case at the success-case price, which is exactly what the current price asks.

Then there is the habit of the calendar. Barjora Line 2 arrived about 15 months late. The UAE line is already 18 to 21 months behind its first public date. Management's financial promises have been kept, repaying the banks early and funding the build without a rights issue, and its commissioning dates have not [1][3]. I do not call that dishonesty; I call it a base rate. When a team has been late three times, you do not assume the fourth schedule is the one that holds, and you certainly do not pay 76 times earnings for it.

Supply is the third worry. India can now make about 22,500 tonnes of capacitor film between Xpro, Jindal's JPFL Films and SRF, against demand of about 15,000 tonnes, and imports still come in at zero duty [113][7]. When Xpro decided to cut prices by 6% to 7% in advance of its own new capacity, it was telling you something about who sets the price. Chapter 4's Jindal and Treofan story is the cautionary tale: a family that built film capacity into a soft market and watched an operating margin of 24% fall to zero.

So I did what I ask you to do with any story you love: I wrote three futures and weighed them. In the bear future, 30% likely, the UAE line slips again and new Indian capacity forces prices down, and the shares are worth about ₹414, which is about 1.2 times book. In the base future, 50% likely, the new lines fill at roughly management's pace at a 30% margin, profit reaches about ₹68 Cr, and at 28 times earnings the shares are worth about ₹811. In the bull future, 20% likely, management's ranges arrive early, profit reaches about ₹131 Cr, and at 30 times the shares are worth about ₹1,674. Weigh them and you get ₹865, which is 24% below the ₹1,142.20 close.

Test that against a hostile question. What if management simply does what it says? I re-based the base case to the management-range profit and gave the bull case more weight, and the weighted value came to about ₹1,197, a mere 5% above the close. In the world where the company is right, the stock is fairly priced; in every other world it is expensive. For the bull case alone to equal today's price, it would need a 52% chance when I give it 20%.

You may think my weights are too harsh, so try yours. Give the bear case only 20%, the base case 45% and the bull case 35%, a far friendlier set than the evidence supports, and the weighted value is ₹1,034, still 9.5% below the close. It takes a combination of the management-range profit, a high bull weight and a 28 times multiple on the base to bring the arithmetic back to today's price or slightly above, and that combination is a forecast that everything goes right.

Let me translate the three time horizons into plain words. If you trade for weeks or months, there is no edge today: the nearest ceiling at ₹1,195.7 is only 4.7% above the close, and a sensible stop at ₹1,105 is 3.3% below it, a ratio of 1.4 to 1 that I would not take [4]. If you invest for the next one to two years, the inflection is real and checkable, because Barjora's ramp, the UAE start and the first margin disclosure all arrive within about six months; but the stock rose 14.6% in the six sessions after the September results, which is the market paying for that inflection before it is visible [40]. And if you are a five-year compounder, the single question is whether ₹700 Cr earns more than it costs, and nothing reported before 2028 will answer it.

If you want to follow Xpro without owning it, I would track four numbers every quarter and ignore the headlines. First, the utilisation of the new Barjora line, which management has said it will report against a 70% to 80% target [3]. Second, the share of dielectric film in revenue, which was 26.8% in FY2026 and has to climb if the margin story is real. Third, EBITDA per tonne, ₹15,127 in FY2026 and ₹16,131 in the first half of FY2027 against ₹27,963 in FY2023 (our calculation) [36]. Fourth, the cash conversion cycle, which stretched from 33 days to 80 as the company stocked three months of imported resin [17]. If the first three rise while the fourth falls, the central case is working.

I would add one more word about alternatives, because a rejection invites the question of what to do instead. The honest answer today is nothing, and nothing is a position. XPROINDIA is not in the NSE F&O segment, so there is no call spread or LEAPS to size a small bet cheaply, and the cash-equity version of the same bet is the one the numbers decline. This report did not underwrite a shortlist name or an outside candidate to the same standard, so the plan keeps the next marginal rupee in cash rather than inventing a destination.

That is why my verdict is REJECTED, and let me be careful about what that word means here. It is not a judgment that Xpro is a bad company; Chapter 6 found clean accounts and a sturdy balance sheet, and Pass 1 rated the business conditional, not failed. It is a judgment that the price leaves no room for error. The usual hedge would be to wait for the stock to pull back to support near ₹1,105 to ₹1,150. But our base value of ₹811 sits below that whole zone, so waiting there gains you nothing. I will only call a price attractive where the reward is at least one and a half times the risk, and on our numbers that is around ₹620 to ₹660, with a stop at ₹560.

The chart agrees that there is no rush. The stock fell 50% from its December 2024 peak, bounced hard, and is now pressing up against a ceiling of flat moving averages between ₹1,120 and ₹1,195, on thin volume [4]. One further day made it look better: after the 13 November close the TradingView print was ₹1,190.10, up 4.2%, but still on 0.6 times average volume and still just under the 30-week average [10]. A clean weekly close above ₹1,200 on strong volume would be the first piece of evidence worth acting on; a close under ₹1,105 would say the retest failed.

What about you? The holdings ledger shows no Xpro shares, so there is nothing to sell and no stop to set; the right action for new money is to keep it in cash until either the price or the evidence changes. I have set alerts for exactly those moments: the price entering ₹620 to ₹660, the Barjora line reporting 70% utilisation with a disclosed dielectric margin above 30%, and the UAE line being switched on. Howard Marks said you can't predict but you can prepare, and this plan is preparation: it names what would change my mind and the number at which it would.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: A rejection is not a prediction that the stock will fall. It is a statement that, at this price, you are being paid for the best case and being asked to carry the rest. Notice how different that feels from disliking a business. The most useful discipline in this chapter is to hold two thoughts together: Xpro may well deliver what it promises, and it may still be the wrong thing to buy today.
